passages.title: A Widow's Second Spring
passages.text:
When Mai's grandmother became a **widow** at fifty, the whole family feared she would be **miserable** for years. Her husband had left a small farm, and a bitter **dispute** over the land soon began between his two brothers. Grandmother refused to take sides. Instead, she moved in with her youngest daughter, Lan, who had **got married** the previous spring. Lan had **married** a kind teacher called Hoa, and the three of them lived together without trouble, because Grandmother could **get on well with** almost anyone. "You do not have to **get married to** a rich man to be happy," she often told Lan. "You only need someone who listens."

Soon a **toddler** arrived in the house, Lan's baby son, who laughed at everything Grandmother did. Watching him take his first steps across the kitchen floor, she stopped feeling **miserable** at last. The land **dispute** was settled by a judge the following year, and the whole family gathered for dinner.

passages.title: Parents of Hanoi: A Survey
passages.text:
A recent survey of family life in Hanoi has produced some surprising figures. **Approximately** four hundred households took part, and **roughly** half of them included a young child. Many parents were **middle-aged**, which the researchers defined as being between forty and sixty. Most mothers were **in their early** thirties when their first baby arrived, while the fathers tended to be **in their mid** thirties. A smaller group, about one in ten, were **in their late** forties.

One father, **nearly** fifty, described how his daughter began to **toddle** across the living room last month, holding on to the sofa with both hands. "I am **almost** fifty-one," he laughed, "and I have never felt more tired or happier." The report concludes that parents are becoming older every decade, and that grandparents are increasingly asked to help with childcare because the parents work long hours in the city.

passages.title: Grandfather's Rules
passages.text:
My father was **brought up** in a village by the sea, and he often says that his own father was the most **strict** man in the district. Grandfather would not **allow the children to** play after dark, and they were never **allowed to** eat before the adults. When Grandfather **died** in 1990, my father was only twenty, and for many weeks the house felt **dead**, silent and cold.

Grandmother, however, was still **alive** and strong. She **managed to** keep the small shop open by working fourteen hours a day, and she even **managed to** save enough money to send my father to university. "People think the **dead** leave nothing behind," she told him once, "but your grandfather's habits are **alive** in every one of us." Today my father is a gentle but firm parent. He does **allow me to** go out with friends, yet he insists that I am home by ten, just as he once was.

passages.title: A Student's First Lessons in Money
passages.text:
Linh moved to Ho Chi Minh City to study, and her first year was a lesson in money. Her parents asked her to **manage** her own budget, so she opened a bank account and, for a few weeks, she was **in credit** and felt rich. Then her friends invited her to a party near the river. Everyone loved to **stay out late**, and when the music started, the whole street seemed to **get wild**.

Linh spent more than she planned, and by the end of the month she had to **get a loan** from a small bank to pay her rent. She also began to **owe** her roommate **money**, because she kept borrowing for lunch. It was not a **tragedy**, but it was embarrassing. Her roommate was patient, and Linh promised to **pay back** the **money** in three instalments, working weekends at a café. "Freedom is easy," she wrote in her diary, "but learning to **manage** money is difficult."

passages.title: A Slip of the Knife
passages.text:
Last Sunday I was cooking dinner in the flat I share with two friends. I was in a hurry because I still had to pay **one month's rent** to our landlord before midnight, and my mind was elsewhere. While I was slicing onions, the knife slipped and I **cut myself** on the thumb. It began to **bleed** heavily, and I felt dizzy.

My flatmate Minh stayed calm. He washed the wound and **put a bandage around** my thumb. Then he asked if I wanted to **take some tablets** for the pain, but I refused, because I did **feel sick** and did not want anything in my stomach. "If the bleeding does not stop, you must **see a doctor**," he said. Luckily it stopped within an hour. Later our elderly neighbour, who had heard the noise, knocked on the door and offered to **give** me **some medicine** she kept for such accidents. I thanked her, and promised to be more careful in the kitchen from now on.

passages.title: Health Talk in Da Nang
passages.text:
Dr Pham, a family physician in Da Nang, gave a talk on common health problems in the town. "Many patients arrive with a simple **ache** in the back or the head," she said, "and they think a visit to the shop will solve everything." In fact, a minor problem can hide a serious one. Men over fifty often **suffer from** high blood pressure without noticing it, and a sudden **heart attack** may be the first sign. Smokers face another danger: **lung cancer** is still the most common cancer in men.

She described a patient whose chest began to **hurt** whenever he climbed stairs. The sensation was so **painful** that he could not sleep, and he finally decided to **go into hospital** for tests. "He was lucky," she said. "We found the problem early." She urged the audience to **go to the chemist** for advice about small illnesses, but to visit a clinic when pain lasts more than a few days.

passages.title: Bargains at the Floating Market
passages.text:
Visitors to a floating market are **likely** to remember the colours and the noise more than anything else. On the morning I went, a woman in a conical hat was selling mangoes from a small boat. A sign **called attention to** her special offer: **three for the price of two**. A tourist beside me tried to **haggle** anyway, saying the fruit was too expensive. In many markets sellers expect you to **haggle over the price**, and they are **likely to** lower it if you smile and stay polite.

Further along, a vendor was grilling **prawns** on a charcoal stove, and the smell was wonderful. Another stall displayed **raw meat** under a plastic sheet, and I noticed how carefully the owner kept it cold. "Customers are **likely** to buy if they trust me," she said. I finally chose the mangoes, paid a fair price, and ate a **prawn** skewer for lunch while the boats drifted slowly along the river.

passages.title: A Wrong Turn in Scotland
passages.text:
Kim, a language student from Seoul, has a **work-related connection** with a whisky company in Scotland, so last autumn she travelled there to practise her English. She hired a small car, and on the first day she nearly made a mistake at a narrow bridge where a sign said **no overtaking**. Later she took a wrong turn and **ended up** in a tiny village surrounded by fields of **barley**, the grain used to make whisky.

A farmer used an unfamiliar word, so she had to **look** it **up** in her dictionary. She was also trying to **write an essay** about rural life for her course, and she took careful notes. She found that Scottish speech, especially the rolled "r" and every hard **consonant**, was harder to follow than she expected. "I want to **pass an exam** in English next year," she told the farmer, "and this trip is my best classroom." He smiled and invited her in for tea.

passages.text:
Diary, 3 May. The final exams start in two weeks, and I must **revise for** them seriously. Last term I did not **do well** in chemistry, and Mum was disappointed. "**Do your best** and do not worry," she always says. My teacher gives similar advice: "**Try your best**, stay calm, and the result will follow."

Every evening I plan to **do some revision** for an hour, mostly vocabulary and past papers. At weekends I **do exam preparation** with my study group in the library; we test each other and share notes. In my school, students who **get a good grade** receive a small certificate, and in my cousin's school in London, you **get a good mark** if you show your working clearly. I do not care about certificates, but I want to prove to myself that I can improve. If I stay disciplined, I will **do well** and make my family proud. Tomorrow I start with mathematics.

passages.title: Planning Ahead for Exams
passages.text:
Teachers in many countries report that students **find it difficult to** manage their time before tests. A new guide published by an education charity offers practical advice. Its first rule is to plan **exam preparation** weeks in advance rather than days. Students who **get through** a small amount of material each day remember more than those who study all night. The guide also recommends that learners **do an essay** every week, because writing under time pressure builds confidence.

Short **revision** sessions of forty minutes work better than long ones, it says. The guide also explains how each **grade** is decided: in some systems the final **mark** is a percentage, while others use letters. Many students worry about this, but the authors insist that effort matters more than worry. "Follow the plan and, **with a bit of luck**, you will see your **mark** improve," says one author. Readers are encouraged to keep a record of their **grade** history in a notebook and to track how their **revision** habits change over a term.

passages.title: Choosing What to Study
passages.text:
Choosing what to **study** at university is one of the biggest decisions of a young person's life. When Nam finished high school, his father hoped he would take **medicine** and **become** **a doctor**, because the family had always respected the profession. His aunt, however, argued for **law**, saying that **a lawyer** helps people solve real problems. Nam was not sure. He loved maths and building models, so he considered **engineering**, a subject with practical projects and good jobs. Meanwhile his best friend wanted to **go into business** and open a coffee chain.

Nam spent a month visiting open days and talking to graduates. In the end he realised that no single choice was perfect; what mattered was whether he could stay curious for four years. He chose **engineering**, though he promised his father to volunteer at a free clinic every summer. "You can **become** somebody useful in any profession," his aunt said, and he agreed.

passages.title: Careers Day at School
passages.text:
At our school's careers day, six graduates described their jobs. **An engineer** explained how bridges are tested before they open. Next, **an architect** showed models of houses and said that **architecture** combines art with science. A former classmate, now **an economist**, told us that **economics** is about explaining how people make choices with limited resources. Then **a psychologist** spoke about children's behaviour; she had studied **psychology** for five years and now works in a hospital.

The most entertaining speaker was **a businesswoman** who started a small bakery after finishing **business studies**. "In class I learned about accounting," she said, "but I learned about people when customers complained!" Our headteacher then asked the group what advice they would give to students: be curious, accept failure, and keep reading. I wrote in my notebook that I might want to be **a businessman** or **an engineer**, though I still have two years to decide.

passages.title: How Memory Works
passages.text:
Psychologists often describe memory as a system with three main **components**. The first is **sensory memory**, which holds what we see and hear for only a second or two. When you **take in** a smell or a sound **from** the environment, your senses send it to this tiny **holding area**, where it either fades or moves on. If you pay attention, the information goes into short-term memory. To **put** a phone number **into** long-term memory, you usually need to repeat it or link it to something meaningful. Researchers say that learners who **transfer** facts **into** long-term storage by testing themselves remember much more.

This links to New Year habits. Many people **start** the year **with a resolution to** learn a language, but few **keep their resolution** beyond February. The reason is that they overlook the basic **components** of memory and rely on motivation alone. A realistic plan, practised daily, works better than a dramatic promise.

passages.title: Five Habits for Better Study
passages.text:
Our guide lists five **key points for effective study**. First, **make an effort to** begin early. A little work every day beats a late-night panic. Second, use an **illustration**: a simple diagram can explain a process better than three paragraphs of text. Draw your own whenever you meet a difficult idea, because making the picture forces you to understand it.

Third, **recite** the main ideas aloud without looking at your notes. If you stumble, you have found a gap in your memory. Fourth, **give** new material **time to soak in**. A walk, a snack or a night's sleep helps the brain to organise what you learned. Fifth, never **cram** the night before an exam; tired students make careless mistakes and forget calm strategies. Finally, choose one weak area and **work on** it every day, even for only fifteen minutes. Small, steady improvement is the real secret of success.

items.explain: 'illustration' nghĩa là Hình minh họa; ví dụ giúp giải thích một ý tưởng, khớp với định nghĩa này.

items.definition: to say something aloud from memory
items.explain: 'recite' nghĩa là Đọc thuộc lòng; đọc lại một nội dung từ trí nhớ, khớp với định nghĩa này.

items.word: give something time to soak in
items.definition: to allow information enough time to be understood and remembered
items.explain: 'give something time to soak in' nghĩa là Cho bản thân thời gian để tiếp thu, hiểu và ghi nhớ thông tin, khớp với định nghĩa này.

items.definition: to study a large amount of material in a short time just before a test
items.explain: 'cram (for an exam)' nghĩa là Học nhồi nhét; cố học rất nhiều kiến thức ngay trước kỳ thi, khớp với định nghĩa này.

items.definition: to spend time improving or doing a particular task
items.explain: 'work on something (N/Ving)' nghĩa là Tập trung làm hoặc cải thiện một việc cụ thể, khớp với định nghĩa này.

exercises.instruction: Complete each sentence with a word or phrase from the word bank.

items.q: The teacher shared some ____ for the whole class.
items.explain: Những nguyên tắc học tập quan trọng: 'key points for effective study'.

items.q: You should ____ get up early if you want to catch the train.
items.explain: Cố gắng làm gì: 'make an effort to'.

items.q: The textbook includes a colourful ____ of the human heart.
items.explain: Hình minh họa trong sách: 'illustration'.

items.q: Each child had to ____ a short poem in front of the class.
items.explain: Đọc thuộc lòng bài thơ: 'recite'.

items.q: After the lecture, give the ideas ____ before you try the quiz.
items.explain: Để kiến thức thấm dần: 'give ... time to soak in'.

items.q: Do not wait until midnight to ____ for the test.
items.explain: Học nhồi nhét trước kỳ thi: 'cram'.

items.q: She wants to ____ her pronunciation every morning.
items.explain: Tập trung cải thiện một việc: 'work on'.

items.explain: Bài nói thậm chí chỉ mười lăm phút mỗi ngày.
